m-communications-overview.title: Communications key concepts: forms and dimensions of communication, 5Cs of written communication, communication skills, trends, tailoring, agile
m-communications-overview.notes: Communication = exchange of information, intended or involuntary (ideas, instructions, emotions), via written (physical or electronic), spoken (face-to-face or remote), formal or informal, gestures (tone, facial expression), media (pictures, actions) and choice of words. Communications = means of sending/receiving via activities (meetings, presentations) or artefacts (emails, social media, reports, documentation). PMs spend most of their time communicating with internal and external stakeholders; communication bridges diverse backgrounds, expertise and interests. Dimensions: internal vs external; formal (reports, formal meetings, agendas, minutes, briefings, presentations) vs informal (emails, social media, websites, ad hoc discussions); hierarchical focus - upward (senior management), downward (team and contributors), horizontal (peers); official (annual reports, reports to regulators) vs unofficial (building profile and relationships flexibly); written and oral, verbal (words and inflection) and nonverbal (body language, actions). Two parts of success: a communication strategy based on project and stakeholder needs, from which the communications management plan is developed; and the project communications themselves (collection, creation, dissemination, storage, retrieval, management, tracking, disposition); strategy and plan also underpin monitoring. Misunderstandings can be reduced but not eliminated by the 5Cs of written communication (for traditional, non-social-media messages): correct grammar and spelling; concise expression without excess words; clear purpose directed to the reader's needs; coherent logical flow (introductions, summaries as markers); controlling the flow of words and ideas (graphics, summaries). Supporting skills: listening actively; awareness of cultural and personal differences; identifying, setting and managing stakeholder expectations; enhancing team skills in persuading, motivating, coaching, negotiating and resolving conflict. Fundamental attributes: clarity of purpose; understanding the receiver's needs and preferences; monitoring and measuring effectiveness. Trends: include stakeholders in project reviews (regular review of the stakeholder community's membership and attitudes); include stakeholders in project meetings, incl. agile-style short daily standups with team and key stakeholders; social computing (infrastructure, social media, personal devices; social networking builds relationships and trust); multifaceted approaches respecting cultural, practical and personal preferences for language, media, content and delivery, effective across generations and cultures. Tailoring: stakeholders internal/external; physical location and time zones; communications technology; language(s); knowledge management repository. Agile: ambiguity and change require more frequent, faster communication - streamlined information access, frequent team checkpoints, colocation, transparent posting of artefacts, regular stakeholder reviews. ITTOs for 10.1-10.3 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 10-1.

m-10.1-plan-communications.title: 10.1 Plan Communications Management: requirements analysis, technology factors, communication models, push/pull/interactive methods, plan contents
m-10.1-plan-communications.notes: Develop an approach and plan for communications based on each stakeholder's information needs, organisational assets and project needs; key benefit: a documented approach to engage stakeholders effectively and efficiently with relevant, timely information; performed periodically as needed. Developed early (during stakeholder identification and project management plan development), reviewed regularly and modified when the stakeholder community changes or at each new phase; also decide storage, retrieval and ultimate disposition of information. Inputs: charter (key stakeholder list, possibly roles); plan (resource management plan - team communication requirements; stakeholder engagement plan - strategies often fulfilled via communications); documents (requirements documentation - may include stakeholder communications; stakeholder register); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance; personnel policies; stakeholder risk thresholds; established channels, tools and systems; global/regional/local trends and habits; geographic distribution); OPAs (policies on social media, ethics, security; issue, risk, change and data management; communication requirements; guidelines for development, exchange, storage, retrieval; historical information; stakeholder and communications data from previous projects). Tools: expert judgment (politics and power structures, culture, change management, industry, communications technologies, legal and security policies, stakeholders); communication requirements analysis (information needs = type and format of information combined with its value; sources: stakeholder register and engagement plan, number of potential communication channels or paths - one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many - organisation charts, project organisation and stakeholder relationships, development approach, disciplines and departments, logistics of how many people at which locations, internal and external information needs, legal requirements. Source note: this edition does not state the channels formula n(n-1)/2; if taught, label it as a supplementary calculation); communication technology (conversations, meetings, written documents, databases, social media, websites; factors: urgency of the need for information, availability and reliability of technology, ease of use and training, project environment - face-to-face or virtual, time zones, languages, culture - and sensitivity/confidentiality incl. social media policies); communication models - basic sender/receiver (ensures delivery, not understanding: encode, transmit message via a channel subject to noise, decode), interactive (adds acknowledge - receipt only, not agreement or comprehension - and feedback/response; noise includes distraction, differing perceptions, lack of knowledge or interest; sender ensures the message is clear, complete and correctly interpreted; receiver ensures it is received entirely, interpreted correctly and acknowledged or answered), cross-cultural model (Figure 10-4: sender's and receiver's current emotional state, culture - generational, national, professional discipline, gender - personality and biases influence encoding and decoding; noise in the medium; useful for person-to-person or small-group communication, not for emails, broadcasts or social media); communication methods - interactive (real-time multidirectional: meetings, phone, instant messaging, some social media, videoconferencing), push (sent to specific recipients - ensures distribution but not receipt or understanding: letters, memos, reports, emails, faxes, voicemail, blogs, press releases), pull (large or complex information or large audiences who access it at their discretion: web portals, intranets, e-learning, lessons learned databases, knowledge repositories); forms of communication: interpersonal (face-to-face individuals), small group (about three to six people), public (one speaker to a group), mass (minimal connection with large, sometimes anonymous audiences), networks and social computing (many-to-many); artefacts include notice boards, newsletters, letters, press releases, annual reports, emails and intranets, web portals, phone, presentations, team briefings, focus groups, meetings, consultation groups or staff forums, social media; interpersonal skills - communication styles assessment (preferred method, format and content; often for unsupportive stakeholders, after a stakeholder engagement assessment), political awareness (formal and informal power relationships and willingness to work within them; who wields power and influence), cultural awareness (adapt strategy to differences between individuals, groups and organisations); data representation - stakeholder engagement assessment matrix (gaps between current and desired engagement inform extra communications); meetings. Outputs: communications management plan (how communications are planned, structured, implemented and monitored): stakeholder communication requirements; information to communicate - language, format, content, detail; escalation processes; reason for distribution; timeframe and frequency and acknowledgment; person responsible for communicating; person authorising release of confidential information; recipients and their needs; methods or technologies; resources (time, budget); method for updating the plan; glossary of terminology; flow charts of information flow, authorisation workflows, report lists, meeting plans; constraints from legislation, technology, policies; may include guidelines and templates for meetings, e-meetings, email, project website and software. Plan updates: stakeholder engagement plan. Document updates: project schedule, stakeholder register. Data flow: charter from 4.1.

m-10.2-manage-communications.title: 10.2 Manage Communications: effective communication techniques and inputs (part 1)
m-10.2-manage-communications.notes: Ensure timely and appropriate collection, creation, distribution, storage, retrieval, management, monitoring and ultimate disposition of project information; key benefit: efficient and effective information flow between team and stakeholders; performed throughout. Covers choice of technologies, methods and techniques and allows flexibility for changing needs; goes beyond distribution to ensure information is appropriately generated, formatted and received, and gives stakeholders the chance to request more information, clarification and discussion. Techniques and considerations: sender-receiver models with feedback loops; choice of media (written vs oral, informal memo vs formal report, push vs pull, technology); writing style (active vs passive voice, sentence structure, word choice); meeting management (agenda, essential participants and attendance, dealing with conflicts and poor follow-up or wrong attendees); presentations (body language, visual aids); facilitation (consensus, difficult group dynamics, interest and enthusiasm); active listening (acknowledging, clarifying and confirming, understanding, removing barriers). Inputs: plan (resource management plan, communications management plan, stakeholder engagement plan); documents (change log - communicate approved, deferred and rejected changes; issue log; lessons learned; quality report - forwarded to those who can act; risk report - to risk owners and impacted stakeholders; stakeholder register); work performance reports (circulated through this process per the communications plan: status and progress reports, EV graphs, trends and forecasts, reserve burndown, defect histograms, contract performance, risk summaries; dashboards, heat reports, stop-light charts); EEFs (as in 10.1); OPAs (social media, ethics and security policies; issue, risk, change and data management; communication requirements; information guidelines; historical information). Tools (part 1): communication technology (factors: colocation, confidentiality, resources available, how culture shapes meetings and discussions); communication methods (keep flexible as the stakeholder community and its needs change).
